etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English prose, from Old French prose, from Latin prōsa (“straightforward”) from the term prōsa ōrātiō (“a straightforward speech – i.e. without the ornaments of verse”).

definitions.definition: Language, particularly written language, not intended as poetry.

quote.text: ...Or if Sion HillDelight thee more, and Siloa's Brook that flow’dFaft by the Oracle of God; I thenceInvoke thy aid to my adventrous Song,That with no middle flight intends to soarAbove th’ Ionian Mounts while it pursuesThings unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime...

definitions.definition: Language which evinces little imagination or animation; dull and commonplace discourse.

quote.text: ...the vehicle is plodding prose, but the effect is none the less poignant. And in regard to this I may say that in a hundred places in Trollope the extremity of pathos is reached by the homeliest means.

definitions.definition: (Roman Catholicism) A hymn with no regular meter, sometimes introduced into the Mass.

quote.text: Proses are parts of the Office of the Mass which are sung just before the Gospel, upon great Festivals. The French also call those Rhythmical Hymns Proses, which are sung in their Offices in the Church of Rome, in which Rhime only, and not Quantity of Syllables, is observed.

definitions.definition: To write or repeat in a dull, tedious, or prosy way.

quote.citation: 1819, John Keats, Otho the Great, act I, scene II, verses 189-190:
quote.text: Pray, do not prose, good Ethelbert, but speak;What is your purpose?

quote.citation: 1896, Robert Smythe Hichens, The Folly of Eustace‎[4]:
quote.text: Already he felt himself near to being a celebrity. He had astonished Eton. That was a good beginning. Papa might prose, knowing, of course, nothing of the poetry of caricature, of the wild joys and the laurels that crown the whimsical. So while Mr. Lane hunted adjectives, and ran sad-sounding and damnatory substantives to earth, Eustace hugged himself, and secretly chuckled over his pilgrim's progress towards the pages of Vanity Fair.
